cards.a: The optional non-transitive attribute that tells a neighbor AS which of your exit points to use for inbound traffic; it is advertised outbound and compared inbound, and lower is better (best-path step 6). The critical exam rule is that MED is compared only between paths from the same neighbor AS unless bgp always-compare-med is set.

cards.q: What is MED's one job in traffic engineering?
cards.a: Inbound traffic selection: with two links to an upstream, setting a lower MED on link A tells the upstream to prefer A for traffic entering you. MED is set outbound toward the neighbor and judged inbound by the neighbor.

cards.q: What are the key MED attribute properties?
cards.a: Type optional non-transitive, default 0 (missing equals 0), best-path step 6 with lower wins, compared only among the same neighbor AS unless bgp always-compare-med is set, and on eBGP the metric is the router's own IGP metric.

cards.q: How do MED and Local-Pref differ in direction?
cards.a: Local Pref is set inbound and means my AS picks the exit; MED is set outbound and means the upstream picks the entry. In short, local-pref influences your outbound traffic, while MED influences your inbound traffic.

route-map SETMED permit 10 with match ip address prefix-list PRIMARY-LINK and set metric 50, applied with neighbor 192.0.2.2 route-map SETMED out. A lower set metric is more preferred by the upstream (step 6 lower wins); for a second link use a higher metric such as 200.

By default MED from one AS is not comparable to MED from another (both are treated as 0). bgp always-compare-med forces comparison across all paths regardless of neighbor AS; use with caution on multihomed connections.

cards.q: How does MED behave across iBGP and a third AS?
cards.a: MED transits iBGP so internal routers know the neighbor's preference, but when re-advertising to a third AS the MED is stripped because it is optional non-transitive, unless it is reset.

cards.q: Command to see the MED per path?
cards.a: show ip bgp <prefix> shows the MED column per path; show ip bgp neighbors <ip> routes and show ip bgp paths also expose MED values.

cards.q: Why might a path with missing MED unexpectedly win?
cards.a: Because a missing MED is treated as 0, and lower MED wins at step 6. A set MED such as 100 is higher than the missing 0.

cards.q: Can MED cross to a third AS by default?
cards.a: No. MED is optional non-transitive, so it does not cross to a third AS unless explicitly reset.

cards.q: Which always beats MED regardless of values?
cards.a: Local-pref (step 2) always beats MED (step 6), and earlier steps like AS_PATH also decide before MED is ever compared.

Type optional non-transitive, default 0, lower wins, best-path step 6, set outbound and judged inbound, compared only within the same neighbor AS, forced with always-compare-med, and its job is inbound traffic selection.
